info.text:
About half of FSA holders forfeited money to their employers in 2022, an average of $441, according to EBRI. This guide walks through the end-of-year money checklist for tax year 2026: what is due by December 31, 2026 versus April 15, 2027; the official 2026 limits for 401(k)s ($24,500, with $8,000 and $11,250 catch-ups and the new Roth catch-up rule), IRAs ($7,500), HSAs ($4,400/$8,750) and FSAs ($3,400, $680 carryover); the 0% capital gains bracket with worked math; tax-loss harvesting and the wash-sale rule; RMDs; the $19,000 gift exclusion; and 2026 changes from the 2025 tax law, including the new $1,000/$2,000 charitable deduction for non-itemizers, the $40,400 SALT cap and Trump Accounts. It ends with credit reports, beneficiaries, withholding, goals and a one-screen checklist.

Sources: IRS Notice 2025-67 (Nov 13, 2025); IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-19 (May 1, 2025); IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-32 (Oct 9, 2025); IRS IR-2015-126 and Publication 969; Treasury/IRS final Roth catch-up regulations (Sep 15, 2025); EBRI, Vital Statistics on Flexible Spending Accounts, 2022 (May 2024); Treasury on Trump Accounts auto-enrollment (Oct 1, 2026); FTC on free weekly credit reports; Franklin Templeton and Eaton Vance on 2026 tax law changes (Jan 2026); Morningstar on SECURE 2.0 RMD penalties.

News and education, not financial advice.
